## Near-Term Climate Action Priorities

<!-- image -->

Guided by the 2013 Climate Action Plan and a review of recent emissions trends and climate actions, we have identified a suite of near-term priority actions, which will help the City remain on track to meet our climate protection goals. These actions alone will not be sufficient to meet our targets; however, they are the essential next steps which will allow us to make substantial progress and will lay the foundation for continued progress.

The actions are transformative, helping us leverage emerging technology and Seattle City Light's clean, carbon neutral electricity to meet the needs of our rapidly growing city. When fully implemented, they will significantly reduce emissions and catalyze an even broader suite of actions over the coming years. It is essential that we implement these actions in the near term to meet the challenge and realize the opportunities of a climate-friendly future. The actions are presented below and summarized in Table 1. Some of these actions will be implemented immediately, while for others we will explore implementation or funding options over the next year with an aim for implementation soon after.

## TRANSPORTATION

Two-thirds of Seattle's GHG emissions result from road transportation. Additionally, transportationrelated fossil fuels are a significant source of air pollution, particularly impacting people of color who are more likely to live near roadways and other pollution sources. As Seattle rapidly grows, policies must aim to rapidly replace fossil fuel vehicles with fully electric options and move single occupancy trips to shared transportation. The overall strategy is to increase active and shared transportation (including biking and transit), accelerate car, bus, and truck electrification, and improve the efficiency of the roadway system to reduce idling and unnecessary driving.

## Improving mobility through pricing

Announce that the City will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.

Research suggests that the most effective strategy for reducing GHG emissions and generating the revenue needed to support transportation alternatives is to put a price on the use of city streets through congestion pricing or some other method of pricing transportation externalities. Road pricing reduces travel times, increases travel reliability, encourages alternatives to single occupant vehicle trips, and improves safety. The Seattle Department of Transportation is preparing a study to investigate possible pricing schemes and how pricing would address an impending congestion challenge being created by tolling in the Highway 99 tunnel, a growing population, and rapid expansion of shared vehicle transportation and urban freight. A successful and just program would support better transportation and mobility access in low-income neighborhoods, as well as pedestrian, bicycle, and transit facilities and services, in addition to transportation demand management programs.

## Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction

Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.

The most cost-effective time to build charging stations and provide the electrical infrastructure for future charging stations is during initial site development. Seattle's codes currently include limited requirements (primarily requiring electrical panel capacity and identifying pathways to accommodate future wiring) that

<!-- image -->

support future electric vehicle charging stations. Requiring new construction to build charging stations and provide the electrical wiring needed for future stations will increase the adoption of electric vehicles and save substantial costs for future charging station installation.

## Charging station network map & strategy

Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018.

While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption. An effective and just distribution of charging stations is critical to realizing the goal of 30 percent of light duty vehicles being electric by 2030, and to support electrification of professional fleets. With significant private sector interest in deploying charging stations across Seattle and the region, a charging station network map which demonstrates the City's strategy and outlines our technical and policy preferences (such as electric grid capacity, race and social justice outcomes, and electrification of shared fleets) will foster the most effective distribution of charging stations and help deploy private investment. The map will guide public and private investment in the network, based on a set of criteria, with a specific focus on equitable distribution of the city receiving significant public benefit when private entities lease space in the right of way. In developing the map, Seattle will work with regional partners with the goal of creating a network the recognizes how people move in and out of the city.

## Ride share and taxi fleet electrification

Work with community and business stakeholders to develop recommendations for making all new forhire vehicles in Seattle electric.

The way people move themselves and goods around Seattle is changing rapidly and, as we continue to advance the percentage of trips taken by transit, bicycle, or walking, we must ensure that new mobility services, such as for hire vehicles, use clean energy to power their trips. As people of color make up a significant number of the operators of these vehicles, it is critical that we work in collaboration with transportation services companies, drivers, and environmental and social justice organizations to ensure that policies meant to accelerate the use of electric vehicles in new mobility are just across the economy.

The city will work with these stakeholders to create recommendations on how to electrify shared vehicle fleets, determine a year after which all such vehicles must be electric, and prepare for the City to begin permitting only electric vehicles for for-hire use.

## Green Fleet Action Plan update

Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.

The City is a leader in fleet electrification with over 200 plug-in electric vehicles, hundreds of conventional hybrid vehicles, and the largest government-owned electric vehicle charging hub. Continued fleet electrification requires a shift in the acquisition and fueling of vehicles and vehicle infrastructure. Electric vehicles have resulted in substantial fuel savings for the city, but they require upfront investment in charging infrastructure. The Green Fleet Action Plan will outline a strategy for infrastructure and vehicle deployment as well as identify pathways for heavy duty electrification, in conjunction with key city departments and with emergency management considerations.

<!-- image -->

## GHG EMISSIONS ASSESSMENT

The single largest obstacle to realizing our climate goals is that the price of fossil fuels does not reflect the true cost of carbon, which is realized in increasing threats to our health, polluted air and water, and damage to property and infrastructure. These costs are disproportionately borne by communities of color and low-income residents. The City of Seattle does not current have a city-wide policy for tracking the carbon impacts of policies or projects, which limits our ability to fully understand the cost or savings related to carbon emissions.

## Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions

Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments.

City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.

## Letter from the Mayor

April 4, 2018

Here in Seattle, we don't wait for others to tell us what our future is going to look like - we create it. We have led the world in aerospace technology, are home to the fastest computers and the cloud, and are pioneering developments to help cure for cancer. And when faced with the challenge of climate change, Seattle is again ready to stand up and lead.

In 2017, when President Trump removed the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement, the City committed to upholding the pollution reduction targets in the Agreement. We know that we are already seeing the impacts of climate change, from wildfires that choke our air to more intense storms that flood our streets. And we know that these impacts are not experienced equally. Around the world, and right here in Seattle, communities of color and lower income communities disproportionately experience climate change.

In response, we must lead with bold solutions that reduce pollution while strengthening our economy and ensuring that the benefits of a clean energy economy are shared throughout our city. Even as our city continues to grow, we must move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.

Seattle has never shied away from confronting challenges, which is why our City will act and do what is right even in the face of such failure from our President. The actions included here won't be easy and will require all of us to work together to get the details right. But I know that when Seattleites put their minds together and resolve to change the world, absolutely nothing can stop us. We can ensure that our City and planet thrive for our children and all future generations.

Sincerely,

Mayor Jenny A. Durkan

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## | Background

In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice. The 2013 CAP included a slate of near-term actions - many of which were completed by 2015 - and more broadly defined longer-term strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.

In response to the Trump administration's withdrawal of support for the international Paris Climate Agreement last year, the City Council adopted Resolution 31757, affirming Seattle's commitment to the goals established in the Paris Agreement, and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) to identify the actions necessary to do our part to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The resulting actions, developed under the leadership of Mayor Durkan, reflect a tipping point in the transition to Seattle's zero emissions future. They are designed to move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.

<!-- image -->

CLIMATE ACTION STRATEGY

## |Greenhouse Gas Emissions

A review of Seattle's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions since 2008 reveals mixed results. While emissions are not declining quickly enough to meet our goals, overall, total GHG emissions compared to 2008 declined six percent, while population grew 13 percent, and per person emissions declined 17 percent (Figure 1). The decline in per person emissions reflects the effectiveness of national standards and local initiatives in increasing how efficiently we use energy, in both the transportation and building sectors. However, while Seattleites are relatively GHG-efficient compared to the nation, state, and county, the modest decline in total emissions highlights the imperative that we fully transition our growing city to a zero-emissions energy supply.

Road transportation made up two thirds, 66 percent, of Seattle's core emissions in 2014. Most of these emissions (50 percent of total emissions) were from passenger vehicles (cars, light duty trucks, SUVs and buses), with the remaining from medium- and heavy-duty trucks. Energy used to heat, cool, and power buildings accounted for about one third of emissions, with that total split between residential and commercial buildings. Waste management contributed three percent to total emissions. (Figure 2) Emissions attributed to buildings has declined from about 40 percent in 1990 and 2008 to about 33 percent in 2014.

<!-- image -->

## Changes in emissions since 2008 include:

- Total road transportation emissions declined two percent and per person emissions declined 12 percent due to a combination of more fuel-efficient vehicles and fewer vehicle miles travelled per person as we have increased transit service and walking and bicycling infrastructure.
- Total building energy emissions declined 13 percent and per person emissions declined 23 percent as a result of lower building energy use, particularly for residential buildings due to lower energy use as our codes became more stringent and incentives spurred efficiency gains. Commercial energy use has also begun to decline, but much more slowly.
- Emissions from waste management remain a relatively small component of Seattle's GHG emissions. Total waste emissions declined 14 percent and per person emissions declined 23 percent, primarily as a result of reductions in the annual amount of waste landfilled.

<!-- image -->

Glò

The pace of reductions between 2008 and 2014 helps us better understand our progress to date and the gap to our goals. Passenger transportation emissions declined an average of 0.5 percent per year since 2008. To achieve the 2030 goal of reducing passenger transportation emissions 82 percent, Seattle would have needed to reduce emissions from passenger vehicles an average of 7.5 percent each year from 2008 onwards. Building emissions declined an average of 2.3 percent per year since 2008, which is on track to meet the goal of reducing emissions 39 percent by 2030 (2.2 percent per year). However, between 2012 and 2014 the pace of building emissions reductions has slowed to an average of 2.1 percent, and an analysis of anticipated reductions based on a current business-as-usual approach shows emissions in 2050 only 12 percent below 2008 levels. 1

Emissions from waste management remain a relatively small component of Seattle's GHG emissions (three percent). These emissions declined 14 percent between 2008 and 2014. Because emissions in the waste sector represent a small share of total emissions and have been declining due to a highly effective program of actions in support of Seattle's zero waste goal, this action agenda focuses on the transportation and building sectors.

While the 2014 GHG Inventory shows some encouraging trends, it also demonstrates that there is more work to be done to meet our climate goals. Total building emissions are declining but that trend will slow without decarbonization policies, and transportation emissions have been relatively unchanged over the past few years. The gap between per person total and total emissions reflects the impact of growth and clearly demonstrates that we cannot achieve our goals solely by being more efficient with our resources. Efficiency remains an important strategy to reduce waste and free up clean and carbon neutral electricity to provide the heat and power needed for our growing city; however, we must rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to zero emissions energy in our cars, trucks, buses, and buildings.

1 Building Energy Use Intensity Targets . Ecotope, Inc. for Seattle Office of Sustainability & Environment. March 2017.

objs.policy_statement: Maintain the City’s climate protection goal to become carbon neutral by 2050 (Resolution 31312).
objs.source_quote: In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312).
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound target adopted by governing bodies.

objs.policy_statement: Affirm Seattle’s commitment to the goals of the Paris Agreement and direct OSE to identify actions necessary to limit warming to 1.5°C (Resolution 31757).
objs.source_quote: In response to the Trump administration's withdrawal of support for the international Paris Climate Agreement last year, the City Council adopted Resolution 31757, affirming Seattle's commitment to the goals established in the Paris Agreement, and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) to identify the actions necessary to do our part to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
objs.extraction_rationale: City Council resolution directing an office to take a defined action supporting a quantified climate outcome.

objs.policy_statement: Reduce passenger transportation emissions 82% by 2030 (stated city goal).
objs.source_quote: Passenger transportation emissions declined an average of 0.5 percent per year since 2008. To achieve the 2030 goal of reducing passenger transportation emissions 82 percent, Seattle would have needed to reduce emissions from passenger vehicles an average of 7.5 percent each year from 2008 onwards.
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound emissions-reduction target (82% by 2030) referenced as an established goal.

objs.policy_statement: Reduce building emissions 39% by 2030 (stated city goal).
objs.source_quote: Building emissions declined an average of 2.3 percent per year since 2008, which is on track to meet the goal of reducing emissions 39 percent by 2030 (2.2 percent per year). However, between 2012 and 2014 the pace of building emissions reductions has slowed to an average of 2.1 percent, and an analysis of anticipated reductions based on a current business-as-usual approach shows emissions in 2050 only 12 percent below 2008 levels.
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound emissions-reduction target (39% by 2030) referenced as an established goal.

objs.policy_statement: Permit installation of publicly available EV charging stations in the right-of-way via a 2017 pilot program.
objs.source_quote: Visible and ready access to charging infrastructure is essential to expanding vehicle electrification. To meet that need, in 2017, a pilot program was initiated to permit the installation of publicly-available electric vehicle charging stations on non-residential streets in urban villages, urban centers, and commercial streets. To date, over 60 applications have been received from three applicants, including Seattle City Light, who installed the first station in February 2018.
objs.section_header: ## Electric Vehicle Charging in the Right of Way
objs.extraction_rationale: Specific named pilot program changing right-of-way permitting to enable EV charging.

objs.policy_statement: Implement Seattle City Light EV charging pilots including installing 20 public fast-charging stations and supporting residential charging.
objs.source_quote: In response to customers' increasing desire for electric vehicles and to understand how best to manage the impact of vehicle charging on the electrical grid, Seattle City Light is designing and implementing two charging infrastructure pilot programs. The programs will expand public fast charging availability and support residential charging at home. Through the right of way charging pilot program described above, City Light is installing 20 public fast charging stations to increase access, while also ensuring that charging is distributed more equitably around the city.
objs.extraction_rationale: Programmatic intervention with a quantified deployment commitment (20 fast chargers).

objs.policy_statement: Require EV-ready electrical capacity in new parking (one EV charging station per space capacity) via Seattle Electrical Code amendments.
objs.source_quote: In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was amended to ensure new parking is built to facilitate future electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The code requires adequate electrical capacity to serve one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show the location of equipment and conduit for future installation of electric vehicles charging stations.
objs.extraction_rationale: Binding code amendment with explicit technical requirements for future EV charging.

objs.policy_statement: Develop a dense network of shared mobility hubs, including accommodating fast charging to advance electric shared fleets.
objs.source_quote: Seattle's Shared Mobility Hub program will aggregate transportation connections, travel information, and other mobility amenities into a seamless, understandable, and on-demand travel experience. The Seattle Transportation Department is developing a dense network of shared mobility hubs throughout the city, co-located with major transit facilities and in places where frequent transit services intersect. A key objective for shared mobility hubs is to advance the use of electric car share and ride hail vehicles by accommodating fast charging at or very near hub locations.
objs.extraction_rationale: Named City program with concrete infrastructure/service deployment intent and EV charging component.

objs.policy_statement: Reduce municipal fleet emissions 50% by 2025 through electrification, cleaner fuels, efficiency, and procurement standards (Green Fleet Action Plan).
objs.source_quote: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement. The City's fleet includes over 200 electric vehicles and over 300 hybrid vehicles.
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified municipal emissions-reduction target with named plan and mechanisms.

objs.policy_statement: Require energy benchmarking and annual reporting for nonresidential and multifamily buildings ≥20,000 sq ft (SMC 22.920) and publicly disclose data (2016 update).
objs.source_quote: Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings (20,000 square feet or larger) to track energy performance and annually report to the City. The policy was updated in 2016 to make reported data publicly available to further increase awareness of building energy use and support real estate market transformation. It is estimated that Seattle's benchmarked buildings represent about two-thirds of citywide commercial and industrial square footage.
objs.extraction_rationale: Ordinance-based requirement with defined applicability threshold and disclosure requirement.

objs.policy_statement: Require commercial buildings ≥50,000 sq ft to conduct building tune-ups for energy and water efficiency under SMC 22.930, with phased compliance beginning in early 2019.
objs.source_quote: Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019. A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements.
objs.extraction_rationale: Ordinance-based mandate with threshold and compliance schedule.

objs.policy_statement: Implement the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program with incentives for early compliance for 50,000–100,000 sq ft buildings (DOE grant-funded).
objs.source_quote: With funding from a Department of Energy grant, the City is implementing the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program providing incentives for early compliance with the Tune-Ups Ordinance. The Accelerator is a voluntary program for owners of mid-size buildings, those 50,000-100,000 square feet, to conduct a tune-up that meets the Seattle Building Tune-Up requirements in advance of when their building is required to comply (2020 & 2021). Building owners can receive Seattle City Light incentives for the tune-up and will be encouraged to go beyond a tune-up by conducting additional energy conservation measures.
objs.extraction_rationale: Grant-funded incentives program; explicit resource-backed intervention.

objs.policy_statement: Convert 200 oil-heated homes per year to electric heat pumps via the Oil Heated Home Conversion incentive program.
objs.source_quote: The Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with clean, efficient, electric heat pumps. By partnering with a heat pump distributor, who provides matching incentives, the program is converting 200 homes per year, while also influencing the home heating market so that electric heat pumps become a preferred heating system. Since its launch in July 2017, 135 homes have been converted with a GHG emissions savings of five MTCO2 per home.
objs.extraction_rationale: Named incentive program with quantified annual conversion rate and electrification measure.

objs.policy_statement: Implement commercial energy code requirements including 2015 SEC criteria addressing emissions via non-fossil heating or more efficient windows.
objs.source_quote: Seattle's commercial energy code (which includes multifamily buildings four stories and above) is a national leader. Approaches implemented first in Seattle are typically later adopted at the state level and in other leading North American cities. An analysis of the 2012 Seattle Energy Code (SEC) found that commercial buildings meeting our code are, on average, 11 percent more efficient than those designed to the national standard, and the current code is approximately 20 percent more efficient.
objs.extraction_rationale: Regulatory building code requirements with explicit emissions-related compliance pathways.

objs.policy_statement: Provide expedited permitting (Priority Green) for projects meeting green building certification and performance criteria including 15% better-than-code energy efficiency.
objs.source_quote: Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections provides expedited permitting for projects achieving green building certification and meeting minimum energy efficiency (15 percent better than code), water conservation, and indoor air quality criteria.
objs.extraction_rationale: Operational permitting incentive tied to measurable efficiency criteria.

objs.policy_statement: Offer zoning incentives for developments meeting the City’s Green Building Standard including 15% better-than-code energy performance (Director’s Rule 20-2017).
objs.source_quote: Multiple zoning incentives are available to catalyze development that is more efficient than code: - Currently, developers can access additional height, floor area, or density In certain zones by meeting the City's Green Building Standard. Director's Rule 20-2017 identifies the requirements, which include - adhering to one of the building industry's green building certification programs and demonstrating that the project is 15 percent more energy efficient than code.
objs.extraction_rationale: Zoning-based incentive with specified eligibility requirements referenced in a Director’s Rule.

objs.policy_statement: Require City-owned new construction and major renovations to achieve LEED Gold and be 15% more energy efficient than current code (Sustainable Building Policy).
objs.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code. In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline).
objs.extraction_rationale: Municipal building standard with measurable requirements; binding for City projects.

objs.policy_statement: Achieve a 20% reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 relative to a 2008 baseline (Resolution 31491).
objs.source_quote: In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline).
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound target adopted by resolution for municipal operations.

objs.policy_statement: Develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
objs.source_quote: Announce that the City will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
objs.extraction_rationale: Commitment to develop a pricing-based strategy (economic instrument) linked to investments.

objs.policy_statement: Pass an electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018 to ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with EV infrastructure.
objs.source_quote: Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.
objs.section_header: ## Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction
objs.extraction_rationale: Time-bound commitment to pass an ordinance requiring EV-ready infrastructure.

objs.policy_statement: Release a map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018 to guide charging network development.
objs.source_quote: Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018. While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption.
objs.extraction_rationale: Time-bound deliverable guiding public/private investment in EV charging deployment.

objs.policy_statement: Develop recommendations to electrify for-hire fleets, determine a year after which all such vehicles must be electric, and prepare to permit only electric for-hire vehicles.
objs.source_quote: The city will work with these stakeholders to create recommendations on how to electrify shared vehicle fleets, determine a year after which all such vehicles must be electric, and prepare for the City to begin permitting only electric vehicles for for-hire use.
objs.section_header: ## Ride share and taxi fleet electrification
objs.extraction_rationale: Explicit intent toward future permitting restriction and electrification requirements; details to be determined but mechanism is clear.

objs.policy_statement: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan by end of 2018 to accelerate municipal fleet electrification and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
objs.source_quote: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
objs.extraction_rationale: Time-bound plan update with explicit fossil fuel phase-out/electrification direction.

objs.policy_statement: Issue an Executive Order requiring City departments to assess GHG impacts of City plans, policies, and major investments, with OSE to define scope/method by October 2018.
objs.source_quote: Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.
objs.section_header: ## Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
objs.extraction_rationale: Binding mechanism (Executive Order) plus implementation deadline for methodology definition.

objs.policy_statement: Prioritize 2019 state legislation to enable a tiered residential energy code that cities can adopt.
objs.source_quote: Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities. Legislation to allow for tiered energy codes will be a priority for the City of Seattle in the 2019 legislative session.
objs.section_header: ## Washington State tiered residential energy code
objs.extraction_rationale: Legislative commitment with a specified session/timeframe and defined regulatory change.

objs.policy_statement: Create a 2030 Challenge pilot offering additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations by 2025 in exchange for deep energy/water reductions and no fossil fuels for heating.
objs.source_quote: Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency. A new pilot will offer additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations in urban centers outside the International District. Projects would receive the incentives in exchange for cutting energy and water use well below code, including no use of fossil fuels for heating.
objs.section_header: ## Establish new 2030 Challenge pilot for 20 upgraded, high performing projects by 2025
objs.extraction_rationale: Named pilot with a numeric cap (20) and explicit performance requirements including no fossil fuels for heating.

objs.policy_statement: Implement incentive-driven performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
objs.source_quote: Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030. Energy use in existing commercial and large multifamily buildings represents approximately 55 percent of the city's building emissions, making a reduction in energy use and emissions in these buildings is critical to meeting our climate goals. Leading up to 2030, the city will work with building owners through incentives, technical assistance and other programs to help them become voluntary early adopters of the standards, and would then phase in performance requirements beginning in 2030.
objs.section_header: ## Incentive-driven 2030 performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings
objs.extraction_rationale: Explicit regulatory backstop (minimum standard beginning 2030) paired with incentives/programs.

objs.policy_statement: Scale Pay for Performance and pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings.
objs.source_quote: Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale.
objs.section_header: ## City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified pilot scope (up to 30 buildings) and incentive-based utility program.

objs.policy_statement: Double budget allocation for municipal building energy reduction and target a 40% reduction in energy use and carbon emissions in municipal buildings by 2025.
objs.source_quote: Double existing budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings from 2012-2015, with a goal of reducing energy use by 40 percent. City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio.
objs.section_header: ## Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025
objs.extraction_rationale: Resource allocation (double budget) and quantified 2025 target for municipal buildings.

objs.policy_statement: Develop recommendations and a financing/incentive plan to convert 18,000 oil-heated homes to electric heat pumps, including support for low-income residents.
objs.source_quote: Propose recommendations to mayor to convert 18,000 homes from heating oil to an electric heat pump OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
objs.extraction_rationale: Quantified scale (18,000 homes) and committed program-design action including financing and incentives.

locals.muni_buildings_sec:
## Municipal Buildings

In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.

In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline). The Office of Sustainability & Environment manages the dedicated funding and works with individual capital departments to prioritize, develop and implement energy efficiency projects. The City is on track to meet the reduction goal, with a 12 percent energy use reduction through the end of 2016.

all_policies.extraction_rationale: Quantified municipal target with defined mechanisms in a named action plan.

all_policies.policy_statement: Require energy benchmarking and annual reporting for nonresidential and multifamily buildings ≥20,000 sq ft, and make reported data publicly available.
all_policies.source_quote: Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings (20,000 square feet or larger) to track energy performance and annually report to the City. The policy was updated in 2016 to make reported data publicly available to further increase awareness of building energy use and support real estate market transformation. It is estimated that Seattle's benchmarked buildings represent about two-thirds of citywide commercial and industrial square footage.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Binding requirement (SMC 22.920) with a clear size threshold and annual reporting/public disclosure.

all_policies.policy_statement: Require commercial buildings ≥50,000 sq ft to complete building tune-ups to improve energy and water efficiency, with phased compliance beginning in early 2019.
all_policies.source_quote: Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019. A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Binding ordinance (SMC 22.930) requiring tune-ups with specified threshold and timeline.

all_policies.policy_statement: Meet the City’s Building Tune-Ups compliance deadline one year earlier than required for private owners (Resolution 31652).
all_policies.source_quote: Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Formal City commitment via resolution to accelerate compliance for City buildings.

all_policies.policy_statement: Implement the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program with incentives for early compliance for 50,000–100,000 sq ft buildings (DOE grant-funded).
all_policies.source_quote: With funding from a Department of Energy grant, the City is implementing the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program providing incentives for early compliance with the Tune-Ups Ordinance. The Accelerator is a voluntary program for owners of mid-size buildings, those 50,000-100,000 square feet, to conduct a tune-up that meets the Seattle Building Tune-Up requirements in advance of when their building is required to comply (2020 & 2021). Building owners can receive Seattle City Light incentives for the tune-up and will be encouraged to go beyond a tune-up by conducting additional energy conservation measures.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Named incentives program with defined eligible building sizes and early compliance focus.

all_policies.policy_statement: Convert 200 oil-heated homes per year to electric heat pumps through the Oil Heated Home Conversion incentive program.
all_policies.source_quote: The Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with clean, efficient, electric heat pumps. By partnering with a heat pump distributor, who provides matching incentives, the program is converting 200 homes per year, while also influencing the home heating market so that electric heat pumps become a preferred heating system. Since its launch in July 2017, 135 homes have been converted with a GHG emissions savings of five MTCO2 per home.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Named incentive program with quantified annual conversion rate and electrification measure.

all_policies.policy_statement: Implement Seattle’s commercial energy code including 2015 SEC criteria addressing emissions by requiring either non-fossil-fuel-based heating or more efficient windows.
all_policies.source_quote: Seattle's commercial energy code (which includes multifamily buildings four stories and above) is a national leader. Approaches implemented first in Seattle are typically later adopted at the state level and in other leading North American cities. An analysis of the 2012 Seattle Energy Code (SEC) found that commercial buildings meeting our code are, on average, 11 percent more efficient than those designed to the national standard, and the current code is approximately 20 percent more efficient.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Binding building code approach with explicit emissions-related criteria; includes efficiency requirements.

all_policies.policy_statement: Provide expedited permitting for projects meeting Priority Green criteria including 15% better-than-code energy efficiency and water conservation.
all_policies.source_quote: Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections provides expedited permitting for projects achieving green building certification and meeting minimum energy efficiency (15 percent better than code), water conservation, and indoor air quality criteria.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Specific administrative incentive (expedited permitting) conditioned on measurable performance thresholds.

all_policies.policy_statement: Provide zoning incentives (additional height/floor area/density) for projects meeting the City’s Green Building Standard, including demonstrating 15% better energy efficiency than code (Director’s Rule 20-2017).
all_policies.source_quote: Multiple zoning incentives are available to catalyze development that is more efficient than code: - Currently, developers can access additional height, floor area, or density In certain zones by meeting the City's Green Building Standard. Director's Rule 20-2017 identifies the requirements, which include - adhering to one of the building industry's green building certification programs and demonstrating that the project is 15 percent more energy efficient than code.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Defined zoning incentive mechanism with referenced rule and measurable energy performance requirement.

all_policies.policy_statement: Provide additional height and floor area for up to 20 projects through the Living Building Pilot Program if projects meet Living Building Petal Certification and other criteria including no on-site fossil-fuel combustion and 25% better-than-code energy efficiency.
all_policies.source_quote: The Living Building Pilot Program provides additional height and floor area for up to 20 projects that meet more extensive green building criteria, which includes achieving Living Building Petal Certification (with no on-site combustion of fossil-fuels), plus energy efficiency 25 percent better than code, and greywater and/or rainwater used for all non-potable water needs (e.g. toilet flushing, irrigation).
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Named pilot program with numeric cap and explicit fossil-fuel and efficiency requirements.

all_policies.policy_statement: Require City-owned new construction and major renovations to achieve LEED Gold and be 15% more energy efficient than current code (Sustainable Building Policy).
all_policies.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Municipal building standard with explicit certification and efficiency requirements.

all_policies.policy_statement: Achieve a 20% reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 relative to a 2008 baseline (Resolution 31491).
all_policies.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound municipal energy reduction goal adopted by resolution.

all_policies.policy_statement: Develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
all_policies.source_quote: Announce that the City will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities. Research suggests that the most effective strategy for reducing GHG emissions and generating the revenue needed to support transportation alternatives is to put a price on the use of city streets through congestion pricing or some other method of pricing transportation externalities.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Commitment to develop a pricing strategy (economic instrument) explicitly tied to reducing transportation emissions.

all_policies.policy_statement: Pass an electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018 to require new construction or renovation of parking structures to be built with EV infrastructure.
all_policies.source_quote: Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure. The most cost-effective time to build charging stations and provide the electrical infrastructure for future charging stations is during initial site development.
all_policies.section_header: ## Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Time-bound commitment to enact an ordinance with EV infrastructure requirements.

all_policies.policy_statement: Release a map of optimal distribution of EV charging infrastructure in 2018 to guide charging network deployment.
all_policies.source_quote: Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018. While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Time-bound deliverable guiding public/private investments in charging deployment.

all_policies.policy_statement: Develop recommendations to electrify for-hire fleets, set a year after which all such vehicles must be electric, and prepare to permit only electric vehicles for for-hire use.
all_policies.source_quote: Work with community and business stakeholders to develop recommendations for making all new forhire vehicles in Seattle electric. The way people move themselves and goods around Seattle is changing rapidly and, as we continue to advance the percentage of trips taken by transit, bicycle, or walking, we must ensure that new mobility services, such as for hire vehicles, use clean energy to power their trips.
all_policies.section_header: ## Ride share and taxi fleet electrification
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Concrete regulatory pathway (future permitting restriction) with a commitment to produce recommendations and set a compliance year.

all_policies.policy_statement: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan by the end of 2018 to accelerate municipal fleet electrification and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
all_policies.source_quote: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles. The City is a leader in fleet electrification with over 200 plug-in electric vehicles, hundreds of conventional hybrid vehicles, and the largest government-owned electric vehicle charging hub.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Time-bound plan creation with explicit fossil-fuel phase-out/electrification outcome.

all_policies.policy_statement: Issue an Executive Order directing departments to assess GHG impacts of City plans, policies, and major investments, with OSE to define scope and method by October 2018.
all_policies.source_quote: Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments. City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.
all_policies.section_header: ## Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Binding mechanism (Executive Order) and deadline for defining assessment scope/method.

all_policies.policy_statement: Prioritize 2019 state legislation to enable a tiered residential energy code that cities can adopt.
all_policies.source_quote: Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities. Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version.
all_policies.section_header: ## Washington State tiered residential energy code
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Legislative agenda commitment with specified session and defined regulatory change.

all_policies.policy_statement: Create a 2030 Challenge pilot offering additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations by 2025 in exchange for deep cuts in energy and water use and no fossil fuels for heating.
all_policies.source_quote: Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency. A new pilot will offer additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations in urban centers outside the International District. Projects would receive the incentives in exchange for cutting energy and water use well below code, including no use of fossil fuels for heating.
all_policies.section_header: ## Establish new 2030 Challenge pilot for 20 upgraded, high performing projects by 2025
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Named pilot with numeric cap and explicit fossil-fuel-free heating requirement tied to incentives.

all_policies.policy_statement: Implement incentive-driven performance standards for existing commercial and multifamily buildings with a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
all_policies.source_quote: Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030. Energy use in existing commercial and large multifamily buildings represents approximately 55 percent of the city's building emissions, making a reduction in energy use and emissions in these buildings is critical to meeting our climate goals. Leading up to 2030, the city will work with building owners through incentives, technical assistance and other programs to help them become voluntary early adopters of the standards, and would then phase in performance requirements beginning in 2030.
all_policies.section_header: ## Incentive-driven 2030 performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Includes an explicit regulatory backstop (minimum performance standard in 2030) plus incentives/programs.

all_policies.policy_statement: Scale Pay for Performance and pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings.
all_policies.source_quote: Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale. To address the 'hard to reach' energy savings, Seattle City Light is developing programs specifically aimed at enabling greater levels of energy efficiency depth in buildings.
all_policies.section_header: ## City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Quantified pilot scope (up to 30 buildings) and utility incentive program design.

all_policies.policy_statement: Double budget allocation for municipal building energy reduction (2021–2025) and target a 40% reduction in energy use and carbon emissions in municipal buildings by 2025.
all_policies.source_quote: Double existing budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings from 2012-2015, with a goal of reducing energy use by 40 percent. City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio.
all_policies.section_header: ## Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Explicit resource allocation (double budget) and quantified, time-bound target (40% by 2025).

all_policies.policy_statement: Develop recommendations and a financing/incentive plan to convert 18,000 oil-heated homes to electric heat pumps, including support for low-income residents.
all_policies.source_quote: Propose recommendations to mayor to convert 18,000 homes from heating oil to an electric heat pump OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: Quantified scale (18,000 homes) and commitment to produce a financing plan and incentives.

o.source_quote: Propose recommendations to mayor to convert 18,000 homes from heating oil to an electric heat pump OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
o.extraction_rationale: Quantified scale (18,000 homes) and committed program-design action including financing and incentives.

locals.muni_sec:
## Municipal Buildings

In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.

In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline). The Office of Sustainability & Environment manages the dedicated funding and works with individual capital departments to prioritize, develop and implement energy efficiency projects. The City is on track to meet the reduction goal, with a 12 percent energy use reduction through the end of 2016.

locals.energy_sec:
## Energy Code

Seattle's commercial energy code (which includes multifamily buildings four stories and above) is a national leader. Approaches implemented first in Seattle are typically later adopted at the state level and in other leading North American cities.  An analysis of the 2012 Seattle Energy Code (SEC) found that commercial buildings meeting our code are, on average, 11 percent more efficient than those designed to the national standard, and the current code is approximately 20 percent more efficient. The 2015 SEC includes criteria that address emissions, by requiring either non-fossil fuel-based heating or more efficient windows. Seattle City Light provides an annual grant to Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections to help make possible the work to develop and implement Seattle's advanced code.

locals.tune_sec:
## Tune Ups

Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.  A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements. Examples of operational fixes include changes to thermostat set points, or adjusting lighting or irrigation schedules. Tune-ups also review HVAC, lighting, and water systems to identify needed maintenance, cleaning or repairs. These types of improvements typically reduce individual building energy use an estimated 10-15 percent. Across the entire commercial building sector, the tune-up mandate is expected to reduce energy use 5-8 percent and GHG emissions by 6-9 percent.

To demonstrate leadership, build capacity in the industry, and help reduce compliance costs, the city has committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting the Building Tune-Ups deadline one year earlier than required for private owners.

dedup.policy_statement: Maintain the City’s climate protection goal to become carbon neutral by 2050 (Resolution 31312).
dedup.source_quote: In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Quantifiable, time-bound community target adopted by governing bodies.

dedup.policy_statement: Permit installation of publicly available EV charging stations in the right-of-way on non-residential streets via a 2017 pilot program.
dedup.source_quote: Visible and ready access to charging infrastructure is essential to expanding vehicle electrification. To meet that need, in 2017, a pilot program was initiated to permit the installation of publicly-available electric vehicle charging stations on non-residential streets in urban villages, urban centers, and commercial streets. To date, over 60 applications have been received from three applicants, including Seattle City Light, who installed the first station in February 2018.
dedup.section_header: ## Electric Vehicle Charging in the Right of Way
dedup.extraction_rationale: Specific named intervention (pilot permitting program) enabling EV charging installations.

dedup.policy_statement: Implement Seattle City Light EV charging infrastructure pilots including installing 20 public fast-charging stations and supporting residential charging.
dedup.source_quote: In response to customers' increasing desire for electric vehicles and to understand how best to manage the impact of vehicle charging on the electrical grid, Seattle City Light is designing and implementing two charging infrastructure pilot programs. The programs will expand public fast charging availability and support residential charging at home. Through the right of way charging pilot program described above, City Light is installing 20 public fast charging stations to increase access, while also ensuring that charging is distributed more equitably around the city.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Program implementation with quantified deployment (20 fast charging stations).

dedup.policy_statement: Require new parking to be built with EV-charging-ready electrical capacity (one EV charging station per parking space capacity) via Seattle Electrical Code amendments.
dedup.source_quote: In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was amended to ensure new parking is built to facilitate future electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The code requires adequate electrical capacity to serve one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show the location of equipment and conduit for future installation of electric vehicles charging stations.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Binding regulatory code change with explicit technical requirements.

dedup.policy_statement: Develop a dense network of shared mobility hubs, including accommodating fast charging to advance electric car-share and ride-hail vehicles.
dedup.source_quote: Seattle's Shared Mobility Hub program will aggregate transportation connections, travel information, and other mobility amenities into a seamless, understandable, and on-demand travel experience. The Seattle Transportation Department is developing a dense network of shared mobility hubs throughout the city, co-located with major transit facilities and in places where frequent transit services intersect. A key objective for shared mobility hubs is to advance the use of electric car share and ride hail vehicles by accommodating fast charging at or very near hub locations.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Named City program with concrete deployment of mobility hubs and EV-charging accommodation.

dedup.policy_statement: Reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50% by 2025 through electrification, cleaner fuels, efficiency, and procurement standards (Green Fleet Action Plan).
dedup.source_quote: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Quantified municipal target with defined mechanisms in a named action plan.

dedup.policy_statement: Require energy benchmarking and annual reporting for nonresidential and multifamily buildings ≥20,000 sq ft, and make reported data publicly available.
dedup.source_quote: Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings (20,000 square feet or larger) to track energy performance and annually report to the City. The policy was updated in 2016 to make reported data publicly available to further increase awareness of building energy use and support real estate market transformation. It is estimated that Seattle's benchmarked buildings represent about two-thirds of citywide commercial and industrial square footage.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Binding requirement (SMC 22.920) with a clear size threshold and annual reporting/public disclosure.

dedup.extraction_rationale: Defined zoning incentive mechanism with referenced rule and measurable energy performance requirement.

dedup.policy_statement: Provide additional height and floor area for up to 20 projects through the Living Building Pilot Program if projects meet Living Building Petal Certification and other criteria including no on-site fossil-fuel combustion and 25% better-than-code energy efficiency.
dedup.source_quote: The Living Building Pilot Program provides additional height and floor area for up to 20 projects that meet more extensive green building criteria, which includes achieving Living Building Petal Certification (with no on-site combustion of fossil-fuels), plus energy efficiency 25 percent better than code, and greywater and/or rainwater used for all non-potable water needs (e.g. toilet flushing, irrigation).
dedup.extraction_rationale: Named pilot program with numeric cap and explicit fossil-fuel and efficiency requirements.

dedup.policy_statement: Require City-owned new construction and major renovations to achieve LEED Gold and be 15% more energy efficient than current code (Sustainable Building Policy).
dedup.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Municipal building standard with explicit certification and efficiency requirements.

dedup.policy_statement: Achieve a 20% reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 relative to a 2008 baseline (Resolution 31491).
dedup.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Quantified, time-bound municipal energy reduction goal adopted by resolution.

dedup.policy_statement: Develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
dedup.source_quote: Announce that the City will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities. Research suggests that the most effective strategy for reducing GHG emissions and generating the revenue needed to support transportation alternatives is to put a price on the use of city streets through congestion pricing or some other method of pricing transportation externalities.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Commitment to develop a pricing strategy (economic instrument) explicitly tied to reducing transportation emissions.

dedup.policy_statement: Pass an electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018 to require new construction or renovation of parking structures to be built with EV infrastructure.
dedup.source_quote: Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure. The most cost-effective time to build charging stations and provide the electrical infrastructure for future charging stations is during initial site development.
dedup.section_header: ## Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction
dedup.extraction_rationale: Time-bound commitment to enact an ordinance with EV infrastructure requirements.

dedup.policy_statement: Release a map of optimal distribution of EV charging infrastructure in 2018 to guide charging network deployment.
dedup.source_quote: Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018. While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Time-bound deliverable guiding public/private investments in charging deployment.

dedup.policy_statement: Develop recommendations to electrify for-hire fleets, set a year after which all such vehicles must be electric, and prepare to permit only electric vehicles for for-hire use.
dedup.source_quote: Work with community and business stakeholders to develop recommendations for making all new forhire vehicles in Seattle electric. The way people move themselves and goods around Seattle is changing rapidly and, as we continue to advance the percentage of trips taken by transit, bicycle, or walking, we must ensure that new mobility services, such as for hire vehicles, use clean energy to power their trips.
dedup.section_header: ## Ride share and taxi fleet electrification
dedup.extraction_rationale: Concrete regulatory pathway (future permitting restriction) with a commitment to produce recommendations and set a compliance year.

dedup.policy_statement: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan by the end of 2018 to accelerate municipal fleet electrification and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
dedup.source_quote: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles. The City is a leader in fleet electrification with over 200 plug-in electric vehicles, hundreds of conventional hybrid vehicles, and the largest government-owned electric vehicle charging hub.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Time-bound plan creation with explicit fossil-fuel phase-out/electrification outcome.

dedup.policy_statement: Issue an Executive Order directing departments to assess GHG impacts of City plans, policies, and major investments, with OSE to define scope and method by October 2018.
dedup.source_quote: Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments. City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.
dedup.section_header: ## Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
dedup.extraction_rationale: Binding mechanism (Executive Order) and deadline for defining assessment scope/method.

dedup.policy_statement: Prioritize 2019 state legislation to enable a tiered residential energy code that cities can adopt.
dedup.source_quote: Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities. Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version.
dedup.section_header: ## Washington State tiered residential energy code
dedup.extraction_rationale: Legislative agenda commitment with specified session and defined regulatory change.

dedup.policy_statement: Create a 2030 Challenge pilot offering additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations by 2025 in exchange for deep cuts in energy and water use and no fossil fuels for heating.
dedup.source_quote: Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency. A new pilot will offer additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations in urban centers outside the International District. Projects would receive the incentives in exchange for cutting energy and water use well below code, including no use of fossil fuels for heating.
dedup.section_header: ## Establish new 2030 Challenge pilot for 20 upgraded, high performing projects by 2025
dedup.extraction_rationale: Named pilot with numeric cap and explicit fossil-fuel-free heating requirement tied to incentives.

dedup.policy_statement: Implement incentive-driven performance standards for existing commercial and multifamily buildings with a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
dedup.source_quote: Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030. Energy use in existing commercial and large multifamily buildings represents approximately 55 percent of the city's building emissions, making a reduction in energy use and emissions in these buildings is critical to meeting our climate goals. Leading up to 2030, the city will work with building owners through incentives, technical assistance and other programs to help them become voluntary early adopters of the standards, and would then phase in performance requirements beginning in 2030.
dedup.section_header: ## Incentive-driven 2030 performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings
dedup.extraction_rationale: Includes an explicit regulatory backstop (minimum performance standard in 2030) plus incentives/programs.

dedup.policy_statement: Scale Pay for Performance and pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings.
dedup.source_quote: Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale. To address the 'hard to reach' energy savings, Seattle City Light is developing programs specifically aimed at enabling greater levels of energy efficiency depth in buildings.
dedup.section_header: ## City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs
dedup.extraction_rationale: Quantified pilot scope (up to 30 buildings) and utility incentive program design.

dedup.policy_statement: Double budget allocation for municipal building energy reduction (2021–2025) and target a 40% reduction in energy use and carbon emissions in municipal buildings by 2025.
dedup.source_quote: Double existing budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings from 2012-2015, with a goal of reducing energy use by 40 percent. City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio.
dedup.section_header: ## Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025
dedup.extraction_rationale: Explicit resource allocation (double budget) and quantified, time-bound target (40% by 2025).

dedup.policy_statement: Develop recommendations and a financing/incentive plan to convert 18,000 oil-heated homes to electric heat pumps, including support for low-income residents.
dedup.source_quote: Propose recommendations to mayor to convert 18,000 homes from heating oil to an electric heat pump OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
dedup.extraction_rationale: Quantified scale (18,000 homes) and commitment to produce a financing plan and incentives.

Meet the City’s Building Tune-Ups compliance deadline one year earlier than required for private owners (Resolution 31652).

Convert 200 oil-heated homes per year to electric heat pumps through the Oil Heated Home Conversion incentive program.
Implement Seattle’s commercial energy code including 2015 SEC criteria addressing emissions by requiring either non-fossil-fuel-based heating or more efficient windows.
Provide expedited permitting for projects meeting Priority Green criteria including 15% better-than-code energy efficiency and water conservation.
